hypothesis: The Voynich manuscript text (Beinecke MS 408) is enciphered natural language. Sub-question: which cipher classes are excluded by reproducible statistics, which are merely unlikely, and which remain live as of September 2026.

claims.claim: Voynichese second-order (conditional) character entropy is far below every European language, so it cannot be a simple monoalphabetic substitution of Latin, Italian, German, etc.
claims.evidence: Bennett (1976) first reported h2 roughly 0.8 bits below European languages, closest to Hawaiian. Zandbergen's tabulation: Voynich H0 3.83-3.87 vs Latin/Italian/German 4.00-4.04; conditional entropy H1 1.84-2.12 (Currier-D, FSG, ZL-Eva, ZL-Cuva) vs 3.04-3.27 (Mattioli, Pliny, Dante, Tristan). Lindemann & Bowern (2021, arXiv 2010.14697): h2 Voynich A 2.31, Voynich B 2.43 (maximal transcription), minimal transcription mean 2.48 vs 294-language Wikipedia range 2.77-6.14; nearest are Hawaiian 2.77, Venda 2.79, Tswana 2.82, Min Dong 2.84; h2 is stable to ~0.1 bit at 10k words. A monoalphabetic substitution leaves h2 unchanged by construction.
claims.source: Bennett 1976 'Scientific and Engineering Problem-Solving with the Computer'; voynich.nu/extra/sol_ent.html; arXiv 2010.14697
claims.counter: Pelling (2017) argues entropy values depend on unresolved glyph parsing (EVA is near stroke-level); Stallings (1998) showed Bennett's Hawaiian sample lacked vowel-length/okina marks. Neither rescues simple substitution: Lindemann & Bowern show every transcription (Currier, EVA, v101, maximal/minimal) stays below all comparison texts, and re-tokenizing into ~50 glyph pairs (Pelling's own tables) barely moves h2 (4.03/4.01/4.04 on his scheme).

claims.claim: Simple substitution plus conventional medieval Latin abbreviation, or of a vowel-less (abjad) plaintext, is also excluded as an explanation of the low h2.
claims.evidence: Lindemann & Bowern built parallel diplomatic vs normalized texts (Medical Casebooks, Necrologium Lundense, Codex Wormianus, Hebrew Bereshit with/without niqqud): scribal abbreviations RAISE conditional entropy, and vowel-less Hebrew remains above Voynichese. Conclusion quoted: the unusual entropy is 'not attributable to conventional scholarly abbreviations or the absence of characters that represent vowels'. Zandbergen: expanding glyphs into letter groups (e.g. one glyph -> 'ius') lowers, not raises, entropy, so abbreviation-expansion 'a very firm: no'.
claims.counter: Nicholas Gibbs (TLS 2017) and several 2020-2026 'Cappelli abbreviation' readings (Edwards; Schechter's 'Latin-Occitan' GitHub) claim abbreviated Latin anyway; none supplies a reproducible key that yields grammatical Latin, and Fagin Davis rejected Gibbs for palaeographic inconsistencies. *Untested residual: non-standard, idiosyncratic shorthand (Pelling's 'Quattrocento shorthand') is not the same as conventional abbreviation and was not in the L&B corpus.*

claims.claim: Currier (1976): the text contains two statistically distinct 'languages' A and B, and the line is a functional unit; this rules out a straightforward encipherment of running linguistic text.
claims.evidence: Currier: words beginning with ct/c't occur line-initially at ~1/10 expected frequency; certain glyphs are line-final fillers (m, g); in ~25,000 words 'not one single case of a repeat going over the end of a line to the beginning of the next'; word-final glyphs condition the next word's initial. His verdict: 'this can't be a straightforward simple encipherment of any linguistic data; there has to be an intermediate step somewhere.' Fagin Davis (2020) found 5 scribes; scribes 1,4 write A, scribes 2,3,5 write B, no hand writes both. Parisel (2026, arXiv 2604.25979): two-state model predicts Currier labels at 89% blind, dAIC 2549 vs one-state, 195/197 folios assigned, dominant feature a folio-level boolean switch on the vowel after ch/sh.
claims.source: voynich.com/currier1.htm; Currier papers PDF at voynich.nu/extra/img/curr_main.pdf; Fagin Davis Manuscript Studies 2020; arXiv 2604.25979
claims.counter: A/B could be two ciphers/key tables, two dialects, or two scribal habits; Zattera (2022) shows the A/B split is a difference in word-internal structure, not vocabulary, with further sub-'languages' by section. Line effects are compatible with a per-line generation procedure (grille, table, or self-citation) but hard to reconcile with a cipher that treats plaintext as a continuous stream.

claims.claim: Voynichese words obey a rigid positional grammar (Tiltman 1951/1968; Stolfi 2000 core-mantle-crust; Zattera 2022 12-slot alphabet) unlike any European plaintext; this excludes ciphers that preserve or randomize letter order within words (plain substitution, Vigenere-type polyalphabetics, letter-level transposition).
claims.evidence: Stolfi's grammar covers >96.5% of text tokens and 88% of label tokens; Stolfi: 'simple Vigenere-style ciphers ... seem to be out of the question'. Zattera: 86.6% of tokens fit a 12-slot template, 10.4% are concatenations of two regular words, 3.0% unstructured (82% of those are hapax); 9 of 12 slots admit only a few glyphs. Rozanova & Temerev (2026, arXiv 2608.17096): order concentrates at token edges (edge-glyph mutual information 0.2 bits, above all prose controls), hapax rate 70% vs 41-60% controls.
claims.counter: Stolfi himself notes the structure is compatible with a codebook cipher, a constructed language, or a syllabic (East Asian) language; Bowern & Gaskell (2022) found that sorting letters within words alphabetically was among the manipulations closest to Voynichese, so within-word anagramming (Hauer-Kondrak's premise) is not excluded by word structure alone.

claims.claim: Letter-level transposition (including Cardan-grille rearrangement of a real plaintext) is excluded; word-level transposition is untestable by character statistics.
claims.evidence: Transposition preserves unigram frequencies and destroys within-word structure, whereas Voynichese has un-European unigram entropy (H0 3.83 vs 4.0+) and extreme within-word order (above). Parisel (2026, arXiv 2604.19762): word-internal right-to-left optimization with left-to-right dependency at boundaries, 80.6% end-class to start-class transition rate; a slot generator cannot jointly reach cross-boundary MI and the transition rate, and a Cardan grille (Rugg's variant) cannot jointly reach the transition rate and Zipfian shape; neither pattern appears in English, French, Hebrew or Arabic controls. Currier's zero cross-line repeats and Feaster's (2022) 'rightwardness' (e.g. Sh-initial words score 0.433 mid-line; ~90% of matched word pairs conform) show glyph choice depends on line position, which no plaintext transposition produces.
claims.counter: *Inference: the exclusion is of transposition acting on letters of a European plaintext; whole-word or block transposition after some other encoding leaves all character statistics untouched and can only be tested via syntax/topic locality (Montemurro & Zanette 2013; Sterneck et al. 2021 find topic clusters matching illustration and scribe, which argues against heavy word scrambling).* Pelling (2009) still posits an 'in-page transposition' for gallows and a 'space transposition' to hide repeats; not quantified.

claims.claim: Verbose (one plaintext letter -> several glyphs) homophonic substitution with nulls is NOT excluded: Greshko's Naibbe cipher (Cryptologia, Nov 2025) reproduces several headline statistics from Latin/Italian by hand with 15th-century tools.
claims.evidence: Naibbe: die roll splits plaintext into unigram/bigram units, card draw selects one of several tables (6 encodings per unigram, 36 per bigram per commentary), output follows an expanded slot grammar. Reported EVA character entropy 3.86 +/- 0.01 and conditional entropy 2.00 +/- 0.01 (VMS EVA: 3.86/2.00), near-identical word-length distribution, matching glyph frequencies and positional patterns; ciphertexts remain decipherable. Hermes (2022) shows Trithemius' Polygraphia III, applied as a random procedure, also mimics low joint entropy and binomial word lengths. Bowern & Gaskell (2022, 22 manipulations): encoding multiple phonemes as bigraphs lowers h2 to Voynich levels for Latin; nulls in some patterns raise word-formation predictability; closest matches are contrast-merging, vowel-removal, affix-replacement and letter-sorting manipulations, with Currier B matching better than A.
claims.source: doi:10.1080/01611194.2025.2566408; github.com/greshko/naibbe-cipher; ceur-ws.org/Vol-3313/paper6.pdf; Hermes, CEUR Vol-3313
claims.counter: Greshko: 'incomplete replication of Voynich B's properties' and no claim the VMS is a ciphertext. Schneier-blog critique (Dillinger): Naibbe was fitted to a linearized text and does not reproduce line-position rules or the manuscript's whitespace behaviour; information density falls to ~1/3 bit per glyph. Rozanova & Temerev (2026): consecutive-token predictability <1% of token entropy vs 2-10% in controls, which they argue is incompatible with padding/expansion ciphers; Zandbergen: contracting glyph groups (Eva->Cuva) raises H1 only 1.84->2.12, so the required expansion is extreme. Bowern & Gaskell warn of circularity and note no manipulated text is as close to Voynichese as other Voynichese subsets.

claims.claim: Hauer & Kondrak (TACL 2016): under the assumption of monoalphabetic substitution + within-word anagramming + abjad, Hebrew is the best-fitting source language; this is a language-ID result, not a decipherment.
claims.evidence: Method validated at 97% language ID on 380 UDHR languages and 93% word accuracy decrypting 50 anagrammed ciphertexts in 5 languages. Applied to 43 Currier-B pages (17,597 words, 95,465 chars, 35-symbol Currier alphabet): decomposition-pattern distance to Hebrew 0.020 vs 0.048 for second-ranked Malay; VMS alphagram-distance minimum less than half of Hebrew's; first line rendered into Hebrew and, after 'a couple of spelling corrections', Google-translated to 'She made recommendations to the priest, man of the house and me and people.' Authors' own caveat (5.4): results are 'either tantalizing clues for Hebrew ... or simply artifacts of the combinatorial power of anagramming and language models'; 'None of the decipherments appear to be syntactically correct or semantically consistent.'
claims.counter: Gorman (wellformedness.com): assumptions unsupported; benchmark snippets below unicity distance; single sentence hand-edited; 43/240 pages. Zandbergen (voynich.nu/misc/misc_01): 35 Currier symbols vs 22 Hebrew letters unexplained; the translated first line is in Currier-A while the model was trained on B; low bigram entropy unaddressed; result not checked across FSG/EVA/v101. Kondrak publicly stated 'We do not claim to have deciphered the manuscript' (2018).

claims.claim: Cheshire (Romance Studies, 2019) 'proto-Romance' reading is rejected.
claims.evidence: Claimed a phonetic script for an unattested 'proto-Romance' with a full decipherment in two weeks. University of Bristol withdrew its press release within a day after 'concerns ... from academics in linguistics and medieval studies'. Critics (Fagin Davis: ''proto-Romance language' is not a thing'; Gheuens: proto-Italic extinct millennia earlier, standard Latin 'Alfonsus dei gratia Rex Aragonum' misread as a Romance hybrid, macron abbreviation misread as a pitch mark; readings inconsistent with his own rules; no reproducible key; no engagement with entropy or word-structure constraints).
claims.counter: Cheshire maintains the reading and has self-published follow-ups; no independent replication.

claims.claim: Bax (2014) 'provisional partial decoding' of ~10 words / 14 signs via plant and star names is not a cipher solution and has not been substantiated.
claims.evidence: Bax proposed sound values from presumed labels (juniper, Taurus, coriander, etc.) assuming an unenciphered unknown language. Pelling: 'every one of Bax's conclusions appeared to be built upon easily demonstrable mistakes'; no statistical account of the entropy/word-structure anomalies; identifications rest on illustration matches that are themselves disputed. Elenigmavoynich (2026) status: 'survives as an interesting hypothesis, not as a decipherment'.
claims.counter: Bax framed it as provisional and testable; supporters note the label-based approach is how Linear B and Egyptian were cracked. No follow-up produced additional consistent readings before his death (2017).

claims.claim: 2018-2026 language-specific claims (Old Turkish/Ardic; Judaeo-Greek/Caveney; medieval Galician/Gladyseva 2023; Latin-Occitan/Schechter 2025; Hebrew-Aramaic web tools) and post-May-2025 LLM-assisted 'solutions' have no scholarly acceptance.
claims.evidence: Ardic family (ATA) claim >30% translated as phonetic Old Turkic; 2025 paper 'The Code Is Deciphered ... How Does AI Assess the Findings' in a Turkish-studies venue; Zandbergen: 'pseudo-rigorous ... readings rest on pure speculation'; Gheuens' 2025 review negative. Caveney's Judaeo-Greek is a voynich.ninja forum theory without publication. Gladyseva's Galician was presented at a Vilnius conference and on Medium. Schechter's GitHub claims '87.8% coverage, 3,648-entry glossary'. arXiv 2505.02261 offers Fibonacci/golden-ratio 'structured decoding'. Zandbergen (voynich.nu/notice.html): 'If you have a solution based on interaction with ChatGPT ... please DO NOT ask me to review it. Since May 2025 there are new ones every week.' Fagin Davis (Medieval Academy): none meets 'the minimum criteria of a real decipherment' (reproducibility, coherent full-text output, peer review).
claims.source: academia.edu/129055807; voynichrevisionist.com 2025/03/25; voynich.ninja thread 2697; github.com/scott-schechter/voynich-decoded; arXiv 2505.02261; voynich.nu/notice.html; elenigmavoynich.com 2026
claims.counter: Proponents argue mainstream researchers refuse engagement; however none has published a key that a third party can apply to unselected folios, and none addresses why the same key yields Currier A vs B or the line-position effects.

claims.claim: Statistical evidence for meaning at the word/topic level (Montemurro & Zanette 2013; Sterneck, Polish & Bowern 2021) supports 'enciphered language' over 'random text', but human-produced gibberish also reproduces most of it.
claims.evidence: Montemurro & Zanette: long-range information structure with optimal scale ~807 words, information profile between English and Latin; keyword networks align with illustrated sections; 'severely limits the scope of the hoax hypothesis'. Sterneck et al.: LDA/LSA/NMF topics match scribe x subject matter. Counter-data: Gaskell & Bowern (2022), 42 volunteers writing gibberish: VMS plausibly resembles gibberish on 41/42 metrics and meaningful text on 38/42; a classifier labels most VMS transcriptions gibberish (low confidence); VMS shows positive word-length autocorrelation typical of gibberish. Timm & Schinner (Cryptologia 2020) self-citation generator reproduces both Zipf laws and word-similarity clustering; their 2023 Cryptologia review of the Malta proceedings keeps self-citation as a serious hypothesis.
claims.counter: Zipf-type and topic-clustering statistics do not discriminate cipher from structured gibberish; Gaskell & Bowern explicitly say page/quire-level structure 'could also be produced by gibberish'. Conversely Zandbergen finds existing proofs of meaninglessness 'not convincing'.

claims.claim: All statistics are transliteration-dependent; Zandbergen's 2022 keynote quantifies the uncertainty and provides a super-alphabet (STA, ~299 codes) and IVTFF format so any analysis can be rerun across alphabets.
claims.evidence: Five main files (FSG, Currier/D'Imperio, IT/Takahashi, ZL/Zandbergen-Landini, GC/Claston-v101). Character-level correspondence between files generally >95% (GC just over 90%); glyph-family correspondence up to 99%. Hapax-legomena share per token ranges 14.1% (ZL all spaces) to 19.6% (GC certain spaces), 'completely dominated by the accuracy of the transliteration'. Bigram frequencies per page change markedly between Cuva-1 and Cuva-2 parsings. EVA is stroke-like and its assumptions 'were likely sub-optimal or even incorrect', biasing downstream analyses.
claims.counter: Lindemann & Bowern show the h2 anomaly survives every transcription and parsing tested, so parsing uncertainty widens error bars but does not overturn the substitution exclusion. Pelling argues no parsing has yet maximized the h1:h2 ratio, so the 'true' token inventory is still unknown.

claims.claim: D'Imperio (1978) catalogued the cipher hypotheses (substitution, polyalphabetic, Trithemius/Selenus systems, Cardan grille, codebook/nomenclator, synthetic languages, shorthand) and found no quantitative basis to choose; Friedman favoured an a priori artificial language; Tiltman's word-structure findings were judged the firmest constraint.
claims.evidence: 'An Elegant Enigma' (NSA, 1978) chapters 4-5; frequency tables but no discriminating statistic; Newbold's shorthand-microscopy reading dismissed via Manly. The Friedman/Tiltman/Currier line concluded the text is not a simple cipher of a known language and possibly synthetic.
claims.counter: Historical, pre-entropy-corpus work; useful as a taxonomy, not as evidence.

claims.claim: Low-entropy natural languages (Polynesian, Bantu, Sinitic romanizations) narrow but do not close the gap; a direct unenciphered exotic language remains merely unlikely.
claims.evidence: Closest h2 values Hawaiian 2.77, Venda 2.79, Tswana 2.82, Min Dong 2.84 vs Voynich 2.11-2.48 depending on transcription; these languages' predictability comes from CV syllable structure and vowel-final words (97% of Venda words end in a vowel), a pattern Voynichese only partly mirrors. Zandbergen lists 'a language with intrinsically low conditional entropy' as one of three surviving options.
claims.counter: Bowern & Gaskell found devowelled Uzbek/Turkish close to Currier B on line-bias metrics but far on entropy; no single language matches on all metrics simultaneously.

consensus_state:
Strongest counter to the hypothesis first: no proposed cipher, including the best current model (Naibbe, 2025), simultaneously reproduces Currier A/B, the line-position effects (Currier 1976; Feaster 2022), the near-zero token-to-token predictability (Rozanova & Temerev 2026), and the word-length/entropy profile, while human-generated and algorithmic gibberish (Gaskell & Bowern 2022; Timm & Schinner 2020) match 41/42 tested metrics. The enciphered-language hypothesis is therefore live but not favoured over structured meaninglessness.

Definitively excluded (reproducible, transcription-robust): (1) monoalphabetic substitution of any European language (entropy invariance; Bennett 1976; Zandbergen; Lindemann & Bowern 2021); (2) substitution plus conventional scribal abbreviation, or of vowel-less European/Semitic plaintext (Lindemann & Bowern 2021); (3) Vigenere-type polyalphabetic substitution (would raise, not lower, h2 and cannot generate the slot grammar; Stolfi 2000); (4) letter-level transposition or Cardan-grille rearrangement of a real plaintext (H0 mismatch, rigid within-word order, line-position dependence; Parisel 2026). Merely unlikely / constrained: verbose homophonic substitution with nulls (feasible in principle per Naibbe and Polygraphia III, but incomplete on Currier B, line effects and token predictability); nomenclator/codebook or constructed language (compatible with word grammar, no positive evidence); an unenciphered low-entropy non-European language (nearest h2 2.77 vs 2.1-2.5); within-word anagramming (Hauer & Kondrak) as a component. Live and unresolved: meaningless structured text vs multi-step cipher. Every published claimed decipherment 2014-2026 (Bax, Hauer-Kondrak, Gibbs, Cheshire, Ardic, Caveney, Gladyseva, Schechter, LLM-assisted) lacks a reproducible key and fails Fagin Davis's minimum criteria.

Checked: primary statistics above were read from the cited papers/PDFs (Zandbergen keynote and entropy page, Lindemann & Bowern arXiv, Hauer & Kondrak TACL PDF, Zattera, Feaster, Bowern & Gaskell, Gaskell & Bowern CEUR PDFs, Currier seminar page, Parisel arXiv abstracts, Rozanova & Temerev abstract). Not checked: full text of Greshko's Cryptologia paper (paywalled; numbers taken from the abstract, press coverage and Schneier-blog commentary), Timm & Schinner 2020/2023 full texts (abstracts only), D'Imperio chapter detail (summary of archive.org text), Bax and Cheshire originals beyond critiques, and the Turkish 2025 journal paper. Items marked with * are inferences. User must verify before relying on any figure; all output is unvalidated until reviewed.
decisive_tests: Pre-registered blind decipherment: a claimant publishes the complete key/procedure; an independent party applies it to 10 unselected folios (5 Currier A, 5 Currier B) and to a control of shuffled-glyph Voynichese; acceptance requires grammatical plaintext in the claimed language at a rate significantly above the control and consistent across both Currier languages (or an explicit, documented key change explaining A/B).

Line-boundary test for cipher class: encipher long Latin/Italian samples with each candidate system (Naibbe, Polygraphia III, Pelling verbose scheme) as a continuous stream and separately with a per-line reset; check whether Currier's zero cross-line repeats in 25k words, the 1/10 line-initial depletion of ct-words, and Feaster's rightwardness scores emerge. Only per-line procedures can pass; a stream cipher that fails excludes that class.

Token-predictability discriminator: compute Rozanova & Temerev's next-token information (VMS <1% of token entropy; controls 2-10%) on Naibbe, Polygraphia III, self-citation and human-gibberish outputs of matched length. If every plaintext-preserving cipher stays above ~2% while gibberish generators reach <1%, verbose substitution is excluded; if Naibbe-type output also reaches <1%, the test cannot separate cipher from hoax and unicity becomes the issue.

Transliteration-robustness requirement: any claimed statistic or decipherment must hold across ZL, GC (v101), IT, Currier, Cuva and the Zattera slot alphabet using Zandbergen's STA/IVTFF tooling; results that flip between alphabets (as hapax share does, 14-20%) are inadmissible.

Unicity-distance computation for the surviving class: for a verbose homophonic cipher with the Naibbe key space (6 unigram + 36 bigram homophones over ~26 letters plus nulls), compute the unicity distance against ~38,000 tokens / ~155,000 glyphs. If the ciphertext is shorter than unicity, no unique decipherment is provable in principle and the field should stop adjudicating 'solutions' and instead test generative models.

A/B key-switch test: fit Parisel's folio-level boolean switch (vowel after ch/sh) as a table change in a Naibbe-type cipher and check whether one switch reproduces the full A/B signature (final -dy/-89 rates, qo- doubling, Zattera's section-specific grammars). Success supports 'two keys, one system'; failure supports two scribal generation habits.

hypothesis: Voynichese (Beinecke MS 408) is statistically language-like at the word and document level (Zipfian frequencies, normal unigram word entropy, medium morphological complexity, page topics, section-level keyword clustering) but is aberrant at the character level and in word sequencing (conditional character entropy h2 ~2.0-2.2 bits vs >2.5-4 for every tested language; rigid word-internal slot grammar; near-absent bigram word order; strong line-position effects; per-folio Currier A/B switch). The natural-language properties it does have are exactly those that human gibberish (Gaskell & Bowern 2022), self-citation generators (Timm & Schinner 2020) and verbose ciphers (Greshko 2025) also reproduce; the properties it lacks are those a one-to-one script of any known language would have. The evidence therefore supports 'non-random, structured, and not a simple substitution of a known language' but does not currently discriminate between an enciphered/encoded natural language and a structured meaningless text; the only features not yet reproduced by any published generator are the 0.2-bit edge-glyph coupling across token boundaries, the ~70% hapax vocabulary, and the large-scale topic/section structure at manuscript length.

claims.claim: Voynichese word frequencies follow Zipf's law (rank-frequency power law), as in natural languages.
claims.evidence: Landini 2001 (Cryptologia 25:275-295) first showed a smooth Zipfian rank-frequency curve; Reddy & Knight 2011 confirm and call it 'a necessary (though not sufficient) test of linguistic plausibility'; Bowern & Lindemann 2021 Fig. 7 show the first 100 ranks of Voynich A and B fall within the curves for Arabic, Bavarian, Occitan and Turkish (Voynich B less of an outlier once chedy/shedy are merged). Most frequent word = 4.5% of tokens in A (daiin), 2.1% in B (chedy); top-10 words = 15.7% (A) / 14.5% (B), within the natural-language range.
claims.source: Landini 2001; Reddy & Knight 2011 (ACL W11-1511); Bowern & Lindemann 2021 §3.3
claims.counter: Zipf is reproduced by every proposed hoax mechanism: Rugg & Taylor 2016 (table-and-grille) report a word-frequency distribution 'that mimics Zipf's distribution'; Timm & Schinner 2020 state their self-citation output satisfies 'both of Zipf's laws'; Gaskell & Bowern 2022 found human gibberish obeys Zipf (though with a weaker average fit, and the VMS also shows a weaker-than-natural fit on the LMZ statistic). Zipf therefore does not discriminate language from structured nonsense.

claims.claim: Word-level entropy and lexical statistics are normal for a natural language.
claims.evidence: Unigram word entropy for VMS B = 9.666 bits vs English WSJ 10.07, Arabic Quran 9.645, Chinese 10.31 (Reddy & Knight Table 1); Adelaide (Abbott group) report 10.46 bits vs a 10.25-bit average across test languages; voynich.nu gives 9.93 bits for the first 8000 words of the Recipes section. Corpus: 37,919 tokens / 8,114 types in the Currier transliteration; ~half of all types are hapax legomena.
claims.source: Reddy & Knight 2011; voynich.nu/a4_word.html; Adelaide 'Cracking the Voynich code' 2014
claims.counter: Gaskell & Bowern 2022: the VMS falls within the 5-95% quantiles of human gibberish on 41 of 42 word/character metrics; gibberish has lower total information content (DEFLATE compression) and higher word repetition, and the VMS shares these. Normal word entropy is also produced by Timm's self-citation model, which generates new variants of earlier words continuously.

claims.claim: Voynichese has medium morphological complexity, closest to Germanic/Iranian (and Romance) profiles; heavily agglutinating families (Turkic, Uralic) and very isolating ones (Philippine) can be excluded; Voynich A is more complex than B.
claims.evidence: Bowern & Lindemann 2021 §3.3-3.4: MATTR (2,000-word window) and top-10 proportional frequency place both Voynich languages in the medium range across 101 languages/7 families, closest to Germanic and Iranian, farthest from Turkic, Dravidian, Kartvelian. Lindemann 2022 ('Crux of the MATTR', 160 languages/10 families, 10,000-word samples, MATTR window 1000, MCW rank 70): Voynichese sits above Romance/Germanic averages and below Semitic/Slavic; Turkic, Uralic and Philippine are statistically excluded by both measures (3 SD), Celtic and Semitic 'possible but less likely'; Euclidean-nearest family centroid = Iranian; A more complex than B.
claims.counter: Lindemann concedes the result 'does not exclude the hypothesis that Voynich is meaningless' because a hoaxer imitating medieval European text would produce similar word distributions, and that the method assumes spaces are conventional word separators. Rozanova & Temerev 2026 show two separator regimes (uncertain separators behave as word-internal junctures; AUC 0.905 on image gaps), and Lindemann notes 45% of running-text tokens differ across transcribers. Timm & Schinner's 2021 Cryptologia review (45:434-438) describes 'severe deficiencies' in the B&L analysis. Family attribution from two scalar statistics is a weak inference (*).

claims.claim: Conditional (second-order) character entropy h2 is far below that of any natural-language text, refuting a one-to-one substitution of any known alphabet or abjad.
claims.evidence: Bowern & Lindemann 2021 Fig. 4: EVA h2 = 2.17 (Voynich A) and 2.01 (Voynich B), lower than all 250 languages in the Wikipedia corpus (alphabets and abjads cluster ~2.5-4.0); the A/B gap disappears (2.23 vs 2.24) when qo- and -dy are removed. Zandbergen (voynich.nu/extra/sol_ent): H2-H1 = 2.05 (FSG) vs 3.23 Latin (Mattioli), 3.13 Italian (Dante), 3.04 German (Tristan), while H1 differs by only ~0.19 bits. Rozanova & Temerev 2026 (ZL transliteration): 2.69 bits vs 3.45-3.52 in Latin/Italian/English controls. Bennett 1976 first noted the ~0.8-bit deficit. Lindemann & Bowern 2020 (arXiv 2010.14697) show the result is robust to EVA/Currier/CUVA parsing and to scribal-abbreviation expansion (abbreviated Secreta Secretorum h2 3.4 vs 3.2 plain).
claims.source: Bennett 1976; Bowern & Lindemann 2021 §2.3.2; Lindemann & Bowern 2020; Zandbergen sol_ent; Rozanova & Temerev 2026 (arXiv 2608.17096)
claims.counter: The fact is undisputed; its interpretation is not. Schinner 2007 and Rugg & Taylor 2016 read the extreme predictability as a hallmark of a generative procedure; Gaskell & Bowern 2022 found human gibberish also has significantly lower h2 than meaningful text. Conversely Bowern & Gaskell 2022 ('Enciphered after all?') show bigraph encoding of letters, null insertion and phonemic-contrast conflation bring Latin h2 to Voynich levels, and Greshko's Naibbe cipher (Cryptologia 2025) reproduces it. Low h2 is therefore compatible with both camps and only excludes simple substitution.

claims.claim: Characters obey a rigid positional 'slot grammar' within words (prefix / midfix / suffix fields), unparalleled in any comparison text.
claims.evidence: Tiltman 1967, Stolfi 2000 (core-mantle-crust), Reddy & Knight 2011 (Linguistica MDL segmentation yields consistent affix signatures); Bowern & Lindemann 2021 §3.2: q only word-initially, m/g/r/n almost only word-finally; Reddy & Knight: letter predictability given the previous letter 40.0% (VMS B) vs 22.6% English, 24.8% Arabic, 38.9% Pinyin. Lindemann & Bowern 2020: 'distinct from every comparison text' because character placement is highly constrained within the word. Gaskell & Bowern 2022: character-position-within-word bias (charbias_words_mean) was the single metric out of 42 that no human gibberish sample could replicate. Stolfi's word grammar fails to parse ~4% of tokens (Zandbergen 2021).
claims.source: Reddy & Knight 2011 Table 2; Bowern & Lindemann 2021; Lindemann & Bowern 2020; Gaskell & Bowern 2022; Zandbergen 2021 grille paper
claims.counter: Hoax side: the slot grammar is exactly what a table-and-grille (Rugg 2004; Rugg & Taylor 2016) or three-wheel device (Zandbergen 2021) produces by construction, and Timm's copy-and-modify rules generate it too. Cipher side: Greshko's Naibbe cipher yields words 'that follow an expanded version of the slot grammar'. Zandbergen notes one 'prohibitive problem' for all generators and all solutions alike: the special paragraph-top behaviour of gallows f and p.

claims.claim: The word-length distribution is nearly binomial and symmetric (lengths 1-10, mean ~5-5.5 EVA characters), unlike the right-skewed distributions of European languages.
claims.evidence: Stolfi 2000 ('almost perfectly binomial' for word types); Timm 2014 gives mean token length 5.5 (4.9 on Currier-A paragraphs, higher in B because of more gallows); Reddy & Knight 2011 Fig. 3 show the narrow binomial shape vs wide asymmetric English/Latin; Adelaide report finds Hebrew the closest match on shape (peak shifted by one). Gaskell & Bowern 2022 add that adjacent word lengths are positively autocorrelated (Moran's I; long-long-short-short), a pattern common in gibberish and rare in natural languages.
claims.source: Stolfi 2000; Reddy & Knight 2011; Timm 2014 (arXiv 1407.6639); Gaskell & Bowern 2022 Fig. 3
claims.counter: As evidence for language it is weak: Reddy & Knight show devowelled English, Buckwalter Arabic and Pinyin Chinese are also binomial; Zandbergen 2021 proves a three-wheel grille with symmetric fragment lengths gives an exactly binomial output and Rugg & Taylor claim their grille yields 'a symmetrical distribution of word length frequencies'; Timm 2014 explains it as a side effect of adding glyphs to short source words and deleting from long ones during copying.

claims.claim: Word order is anomalously weak: a word is barely more predictable from its predecessor than from unigram frequency, and repeated word bigrams/trigrams are rare.
claims.evidence: Reddy & Knight 2011 Table 4: bigram context improves word prediction by 8.85% for VMS B vs 151% English, 252% Arabic, 123% Hungarian (chosen as a free-word-order control). Adelaide 2014: bigram word entropy 14.81 bits, near the maximum in their set (Chinese 14.83) despite normal unigram entropy. Rozanova & Temerev 2026: adjacent-token mutual information is 0.79% of token entropy vs 2.02-15.81% in prose, cipher and pseudo-text controls, and 'order sits at the edges of tokens ... not in the succession of tokens'. Reddy & Knight Fig. 5: almost no long-range collocation (PMI) beyond distance 1.
claims.counter: Pro-language side: Bowern & Lindemann 2021 §4.2 list a few syntagmatic regularities (in Voynich B a qo- word is usually preceded by a -y word; aiin is preceded by 1-2 letter words; gallows preceded by o-), and a verbose/homophonic cipher that renders one plaintext word as many ciphertext variants would dilute bigram statistics; the Naibbe cipher reproduces weak token order. But Timm 2014 treats weak word order plus similarity-based clustering as decisive against any language or conlang, and self-citation also reproduces it (Rozanova & Temerev). Currently the weak-order fact counts against a plaintext reading and is neutral between cipher and hoax.

claims.claim: There is unusually strong statistical coupling across word boundaries (last glyphs of a word predict the first glyphs of the next), stronger than within-token order.
claims.evidence: Currier 1976 first observation; Reddy & Knight 2011 Table 5: the last character of the previous word improves prediction of the first character by 31.8% (comparable to English 31.1%). Parisel 2026 (arXiv 2604.19762): end-to-start boundary transition rate 80.6% vs 19.8-35.5% in English/French/Hebrew/Arabic; cross-boundary MI 0.230 bits (0.586 in Currier A) vs 0.054-0.173; 97% of that MI sits in specific grapheme pairs, not classes; 'bilateral positional extremity' (q, iin ratios >100:1). Rozanova & Temerev 2026: 0.197 bits final-to-initial glyph MI vs 0.067 bits between token identities, reversing the prose pattern.
claims.counter: Parisel shows a surface Markov model reproduces the directional dissociation (10/10 runs), so it is 'non-diagnostic', and neither slot-based nor Cardan-grille generators reproduce all four boundary signatures jointly; he reads the result as cipher-like rather than linguistic. Rozanova & Temerev find neither the Naibbe cipher nor a self-citation generator reproduces the edge coupling, so it is currently unexplained by any camp. Hoax-side caveat: since ~half of separators are 'uncertain' and behave like internal junctures, some boundary coupling may be intra-word structure misread as syntax (*).

claims.claim: Adjacent repetition of identical words is elevated but within natural-language range.
claims.evidence: Bowern & Lindemann 2021 §4.2: probability that a word repeats its predecessor = 0.84% (A) and 0.94% (B); corpus range 0.02-4.8%, mean 0.63%, but 0.25-0.37% for the relevant families (Germanic, Romance, Iranian, Semitic). Sequences such as 'qokedy qokedy qokedy' and 'dar dar' are common (Reddy & Knight; Stolfi).
claims.counter: Gaskell & Bowern 2022: higher repeated_words and tripled_words are significant markers of gibberish vs meaningful text, and the VMS shares them; Barlow 1986 and Rugg cite adjacent near-duplicates as the classic hoax symptom. Bowern & Lindemann's own comparison shows the VMS is 2-4x the rate of the language families they otherwise find closest.

claims.claim: Similarly spelled words cluster locally (same line / preceding lines) and word similarity correlates with frequency, which a 'self-citation' copying process reproduces along with Zipf, line effects and binomial lengths (hoax hypothesis).
claims.evidence: Schinner 2007 (Cryptologia 31:2): random-walk mapping shows positive long-range correlations beyond ~72 characters (about one line) unlike Latin/German, and the recurrence of similar tokens follows a geometric distance distribution; text more consistent with a quasi-stochastic (Rugg-type) process. Timm 2014 / Timm & Schinner 2020 (Cryptologia 44:1-19): similar words concentrate within the previous ~20 lines; second word shorter than first in 48% of lines vs longer in 32%; 62% of m-glyph occurrences line-final; a concrete hand-executable algorithm reproduces both Zipf laws, the binomial length distribution, first/last-word effects, and A/B as process drift (B more repetitive, written later).
claims.source: Schinner 2007; Timm 2014 (arXiv 1407.6639); Timm & Schinner 2020; Timm & Schinner 2023 (Cryptologia 48:4)
claims.counter: Bowern & Lindemann 2021: gibberish cannot explain higher-level document structure (topics, section keywords, page adjacency). Rozanova & Temerev 2026 tested a self-citation generator directly: it reproduces low entropy, weak token order and the null substitution-attack result but fails to produce the 0.2-bit edge-glyph coupling, the ~70% hapax vocabulary, or the graded space structure. Zandbergen 2021: no generator yet accounts for the paragraph-top restriction of f/p. Reddy & Knight: Schinner's observations 'only confirm that the VMS has some properties unlike natural language, but not that it is necessarily a hoax'.

claims.claim: Long-range information structure: content-like keywords cluster across sections at the same scale as in natural-language texts (Montemurro & Zanette), and network/intermittency metrics are compatible with natural languages and incompatible with shuffled text (Amancio et al.).
claims.evidence: Montemurro & Zanette 2013 (PLoS ONE 8:e66344): the entropy-based information measure peaks at a domain scale of ~807 words (natural languages 600-800; unlike DNA or Fortran); magnitude slightly above English, well below Chinese (~0.2-0.6 bits/word range); all 30 top keywords (shedy 0.0094 bits, qokeedy 0.0084, daiin 0.0078, chedy 0.0072 ...) significant at p<0.01 vs shuffled text; strongest inter-section link Pharmacological-Herbal, then Recipes-Astrological. Amancio et al. 2013 (PLoS ONE 8:e67310): intermittency (~1.4-1.9 SD distance), degree (~0.95) and shortest paths (~1.07) separate VMS from its shuffled versions; VMS 'compatible with natural languages for most of the measurements' against the New Testament in 15 languages + Esperanto. Landini 2001: spectral analysis of the space-less text shows natural-language-like structure and recovers the modal token length.
claims.source: Montemurro & Zanette 2013; Amancio et al. 2013; Landini 2001
claims.counter: The null model is wrong: both papers compare against shuffled text, and Gaskell & Bowern 2022 argue the proper null is human-produced gibberish, whose word-placement bias within a sample (wordbias_mean) already matches or exceeds meaningful text and whose properties would drift over months of writing, producing section-level clustering; self-citation copies vocabulary from the current section by construction. Pelling (Cipher Mysteries 2013) argues the 30 'informative' words may be the least informative (cipher container layer) and that M&Z assume a homogeneity across A/B that does not hold. M&Z's argument that these features were 'out of reach of sixteenth-century mathematics' is a non sequitur: a generative procedure need not be aware of the statistics it produces. Amancio also assume no polyalphabetic encryption.

claims.claim: Pages have topics and are in order: within-page word bursts and adjacent-page similarity match meaningful texts, and unsupervised topic models align with illustration sections and scribal hands.
claims.evidence: Reddy & Knight 2011: topicality 1-T/Trand = 0.037 (VMS B) vs 0.033 WSJ, 0.069 Genesis, 0.025 Quran; ADJPAGESIM (nearest bag-of-words neighbour is an adjacent page) = 38.8% for VMS B and 15.6% overall vs 0% when pages are scrambled, 25.0% Genesis, 27.5% Quran, 0.44% WSJ. Sterneck, Polish & Bowern 2021 (arXiv 2107.02858): LDA/LSA/NMF clusters 'match closely to a conjunction of scribe and subject matter' (Davis 2020's five hands); NMF topic 0 tracks the balneological section, recipes and botanicals are distinct topics.
claims.source: Reddy & Knight 2011 Tables 6-7; Sterneck et al. 2021; Bowern & Lindemann 2021 §4.3
claims.counter: Scribe and topic are confounded (scribe 1 = Voynich A herbal; scribes 2-5 = B), so clusters may reflect individual scribal habits or vocabulary drift rather than content; Gaskell & Bowern 2022 explicitly say gibberish at manuscript length has not been tested and that participants spontaneously reused an invented 'label' word around its illustration ('pitshol'). Currier A/B vocabulary differences alone would produce section-level clustering. No quantitative purity/agreement metric is reported by Sterneck et al. (*).

claims.claim: The line is a functional unit: word length and glyph choice depend on position in the line and paragraph, unlike prose.
claims.evidence: Currier 1976; Vogt 2012 ('The Line as a Functional Unit'): across Currier/Takahashi/Stolfi transcriptions the first word is longer than average, the second shorter, and mean length falls ~0.5-1.0 characters (~0.7) along the line; natural-language controls (Latin De bello gallico, German/English Tom Sawyer, French, Italian) show only a ~0.1-character first-word excess and no second-word dip. Bowern & Lindemann 2021: ~85% of paragraphs begin with a gallows (t,k,f,p); line-initial s- variants (saiin/sol/sor for aiin/ol/or), line-final -m/-g variants (dam/am for daiin/aiin); Reddy & Knight Fig. 7: low-frequency glyphs concentrate at line ends, high-frequency at line starts.
claims.source: Currier 1976; Vogt 2012; Reddy & Knight 2011; Bowern & Lindemann 2021 §4.1
claims.counter: Interpretation splits three ways. Bowern & Lindemann treat the effects as 'typographical' positional allographs comparable to scribal punctuation, i.e. compatible with encoded language. Timm 2014 derives them from copying the first/last word of the line above. Gaskell & Bowern 2022 found character-position-in-line bias is the single most important variable separating gibberish from meaningful text, but the VMS value was not significantly different from meaningful text on that metric. Vogt attributes the overall length drop-off to a 'short words make long lines' selection effect present in natural text too.

claims.claim: The Currier A/B distinction is real and reduces largely to a per-folio binary switch in a few character-pair choices, with the same slot grammar in both.
claims.evidence: Currier 1976; Bowern & Lindemann 2021: top-10 vocabularies differ substantially (daiin/chol/chor vs chedy/ol/shedy), B has ~2x qo- and ~3x -dy; scribe 1 writes A, scribes 2-5 write B (Davis 2020). Parisel 2026 (arXiv 2604.25979): a Beta-Binomial mixture on 11 character-pair substitution ratios over 185 folios selects 2 components by BIC and predicts held-out Currier labels at 89.2% without seeing them; the dominant component is a boolean switch, set once per folio, governing the vowel after ch/sh (two-state model ΔAIC = 2,549; 195/197 folios assigned unambiguously; word-template identity explains 92% of variance, with fixed vs switchable contexts). Lindemann 2022: A more morphologically complex than B by MATTR/MCW.
claims.counter: A per-folio boolean switch in a phoneme-like slot looks more like a cipher key or scribal convention than a dialect difference (Parisel reads it as a 'low-resolution projection of a higher-dimensional generative system'); Timm & Schinner explain A vs B as drift and increasing repetitiveness of the copying process over time (B written later, more repetitive); Bowern & Lindemann themselves say A and B are 'two methods of encoding at least one natural language' rather than two languages.

claims.claim: The character stream is optimized right-to-left at the n-gram level even though the manuscript is written left-to-right.
claims.evidence: Parisel 2025 (arXiv 2509.10573): perplexity asymmetry Δ = X_LTR - X_RTL is positive for EVA Voynich at n=2 (+0.0653, 95% CI 0.0631-0.0677), n=3 (+0.0167) and n=4 (+0.0058), with 1,000 bootstrap resamples; English and French are negative (-0.003 to -0.12), Hebrew/Arabic inconsistent across orders; shuffle controls remove the signal; 73.9% next-glyph prediction accuracy at n=4. The grapheme boundary distribution is Zipfian rather than plateau-shaped as in natural languages.
claims.counter: The author concedes the RTL signal 'could be a byproduct of a cipher or a scribal artifact rather than a natural language', the comparison set is four languages, and Hebrew/Arabic themselves fail to show a consistent RTL signature under the method, which undermines its validity as a directionality detector. Single transcription (EVA) only.

claims.claim: Voynichese is an abjad (consonant-only script), explaining the binomial word lengths and the two-class letter structure.
claims.evidence: Reddy & Knight 2011: a two-state bigram HMM over letters puts the last character of every word in one state and all others in the other (grammar ab+), the same pattern learned on undiacritized Arabic and devowelled English; binomial word-length shape matches Buckwalter Arabic and devowelled English; Hauer & Kondrak 2016 (TACL 4:75-86) find Hebrew the best anagram-pattern match among 380 languages.
claims.counter: Bowern & Lindemann 2021: abjads have higher h2 than alphabets (Hebrew/Arabic ~3.5-4 per Zandbergen's ranges), whereas Voynichese is lower; almost every Voynich word contains one of the Sukhotin 'vowels' (a, o, e, h, i), unlike abjad text; the HMM split is likely driven by word-final-only glyphs (m, n, g), i.e. positional allographs, not vowel loss. Hauer & Kondrak produced no grammatical sentences; Bowern & Lindemann call the Hebrew claim 'unconvincing'. Lindemann 2022 ranks Semitic as 'possible but less likely' by MATTR/MCW.

claims.claim: Voynichese is a syllabary-like or verbose (many-to-one / homophonic) encoding of a European language, which would reconcile normal word-level statistics with abnormal character-level statistics.
claims.evidence: Bowern & Lindemann 2021 conclude the script 'is not structure-preserving in that the graphemes are not one-to-one' and that only manipulations conflating phonemic distinctions reach Voynich h2. Bowern & Gaskell 2022 (CEUR paper6): of 22 manipulations, encoding letters as bigraphs, adding nulls in patterns, devowelling, and merging place/manner/voicing contrasts bring Latin, Uzbek and Turkish texts closest to Voynich metrics (Currier B matches better than A). Greshko 2025 (Cryptologia, Naibbe cipher): a dice-and-cards verbose homophonic substitution encrypts Latin/Italian into decipherable text that 'reproduce[s] many key statistical properties of the Voynich Manuscript at once', incompletely for Voynich B. Rozanova & Temerev 2026: BPE finds an optimal unit scale of ~64 merges (88 multi-glyph units of ~2.4 glyphs) that survives space erasure, and Naibbe reproduces entropy, unit scale and token order. voynich.nu 'Key' analysis: stripping positional affixes leaves roots with h2 in the 2.0-2.5 syllabary band (*not independently verified).
claims.source: Bowern & Lindemann 2021 §6; Bowern & Gaskell 2022; Greshko 2025; Rozanova & Temerev 2026
claims.counter: Bowern & Gaskell 2022 found no single manipulation matches Voynich on all metrics and that 'no manuscript is as close as the other samples of Voynichese'; several gibberish samples were equidistant with the enciphered Latin. Rozanova & Temerev: concatenative homophonic ciphers (1-3 symbols/letter) are rejected (language-match differential +0.13 to +0.52 vs Voynich -0.15 to +0.08) and Naibbe lacks the edge-glyph coupling and hapax-rich vocabulary. Zandbergen (sol_ent) notes expanding characters verbosely lowers rather than raises entropy, which constrains which verbose schemes are viable. A verbose cipher must also explain why 15th-century plaintext would leave no decipherable trace after a century of attack.

claims.claim: Long-range correlation/Hurst-type statistics do not match any single natural language.
claims.evidence: Landini 2001: spectral analysis (1/f-like) indicates non-random, language-like long-range organization. Schinner 2007: bit-sequence random walk shows positive correlations building beyond ~1 line, unlike Latin/German. Arutyunov et al. 2016 (arXiv 1611.09122): Hurst exponents of inter-occurrence distances of frequent letters are <0.5 (antipersistent) with sharp unimodal peaks for every natural and constructed language tested (Klingon, Elvish, Esperanto included); the Voynich distribution is shifted right and flatter, i.e. symbols placed 'more randomly', not matching one language; they suggest a two-language mixture and reject their own Danish/Spanish letter-frequency match.
claims.counter: Methods are heterogeneous (character series with/without spaces, binary encodings), sensitive to transcription and sample length, and no study reports a Voynich Hurst exponent with confidence intervals against matched-length controls; the same 'beyond one line' correlation is what self-citation from the line above predicts (Timm & Schinner). Gaskell & Bowern's positive word-length autocorrelation is the only long-range statistic tested against human gibberish, and it favoured gibberish.

claims.claim: The vocabulary is open and hapax-rich, yet built from a closed set of near-neighbour variants.
claims.evidence: 8,114 types / 37,919 tokens (Currier transliteration; Reddy & Knight); ~half of types occur once (voynich.nu); Rozanova & Temerev 2026: 7,022 distinct forms with 70% singleton types in the ZL transliteration; Timm 2014: a grid of words occurring >=4 times covers 80% of the text, with most tokens at edit distance 1 from a frequent word; Bowern & Lindemann: most frequent words have 4-5 letters rather than the 1-3 typical of function words.
claims.source: Reddy & Knight 2011; voynich.nu/a4_word.html; Timm 2014; Rozanova & Temerev 2026
claims.counter: For the hoax side, Timm's copy-and-modify process naturally yields many one-off variants ('strange words usually occur only once'); for the language side, Lindemann 2022 reports the hapax proportion is 'middle range' among languages. Rozanova & Temerev found neither their self-citation generator nor Naibbe reproduced the 70% hapax rate, so this is presently unexplained by any tested model; it is also inflated by uncertain word spaces and transcription disagreement (45% of tokens).

claims.claim: At the sub-paragraph scale Voynichese is statistically closer to human-produced meaningless text than to meaningful text (Gaskell & Bowern 2022).
claims.evidence: 42 volunteers wrote 1-3 pages of invented 'gibberish'; 42 metrics on 200-word excerpts vs 75 meaningful texts (5.6M words) and five VMS transcriptions/subsets. Gibberish replicated meaningful text on all 42 metrics (36 probable, 6 plausible); the VMS plausibly resembled meaningful text on 38/42 and gibberish on 41/42. Gibberish had significantly lower information content and h2, more repeated/tripled words and characters, higher positional bias of words within a sample, positive word-length autocorrelation and weaker Zipf fit, and all of these except line-position character bias were also significant in the VMS. A random forest classified all five VMS samples as gibberish (score <0.5, low confidence). Only within-word character-position bias could not be produced by gibberish writers.
claims.source: Gaskell & Bowern 2022 (CEUR Vol-3313 paper4; data at github.com/danielgaskell/voynich)
claims.counter: The authors state the study 'cannot and does not attempt to prove that the VMS is gibberish'; samples are too short to test topic/section structure, which 'pose[s] a serious challenge to proponents of the hoax hypothesis'; 20 of 42 participants had been taught VMS statistics (contamination effects found small); Latin-alphabet writing cannot mimic Voynich glyph typography; and the companion paper (Bowern & Gaskell 2022) shows several phoneme-conflating ciphers of Latin/Uzbek land equally close to the VMS, so proximity to gibberish is not proximity to gibberish alone. Bowern & Lindemann 2021 (fn. 4) report that sustained language-like nonsense becomes very difficult beyond ~100 words.

consensus_state: No consensus, but the disagreement has narrowed to a specific shape. Agreed facts (all camps): Zipfian word frequencies; normal unigram word entropy and top-word proportions; medium MATTR/type-token profile; near-binomial word lengths; h2 of ~2.0-2.2 bits (EVA) far below every tested language; rigid word-internal slot grammar; near-absent bigram word order but strong glyph coupling across word boundaries; line- and paragraph-position effects; a real Currier A/B split now shown to be largely a per-folio switch; page-level topics and adjacent-page similarity. Interpretive camps: (1) Yale group (Bowern, Lindemann, Sterneck; Annual Review 2021) - enciphered/encoded natural language of medium morphological complexity in a non-structure-preserving script, with the document-level structure as the key argument; but Bowern's own 2022 papers concede that low-level statistics are reproduced by human gibberish and that the correct null model is gibberish, not shuffled text, and that no tested cipher matches Voynichese on all metrics. (2) Hoax/structured-nonsense camp (Rugg & Taylor 2016; Schinner 2007; Timm & Schinner 2020, 2023, and their 2021 Cryptologia review calling B&L deficient) - self-citation or grille generation reproduces Zipf, binomial lengths, line effects and A/B; not yet shown to reproduce section keywords at manuscript length, edge-glyph coupling, or the hapax profile. (3) 2025-2026 quantitative wave (Greshko's Naibbe cipher; Parisel's directional/boundary and A/B-switch papers; Rozanova & Temerev's units paper) - converging on 'cipher-like layered constraints' in which glyphs are not letters, tokens are not words and spaces are not uniform, with both a verbose homophonic cipher and a self-citation generator reproducing the entropy/unit-scale/weak-order profile and both failing on edge coupling and vocabulary openness. Net: the evidence excludes random text, a one-to-one substitution of any known language, heavily agglutinating or purely isolating plaintexts if tokens are words, and simple grille output; it does not currently discriminate enciphered language from structured meaninglessness. Checked: primary texts of Bowern & Lindemann 2021, Gaskell & Bowern 2022, Bowern & Gaskell 2022, Lindemann 2022, Reddy & Knight 2011, Timm 2014, Vogt 2012, Zandbergen 2021, Arutyunov 2016, Sterneck et al. 2021 (full text), plus abstracts/summaries of Montemurro & Zanette 2013, Amancio 2013, Parisel 2025/2026, Rozanova & Temerev 2026, Timm & Schinner 2020/2023, Schinner 2007, Landini 2001, Greshko 2025. Not checked: full text of Rugg & Taylor 2016, Schinner 2007, Landini 2001, Greshko 2025, Timm & Schinner 2021 review and 2023 discussion (paywalled); Parisel and Rozanova & Temerev numbers taken from arXiv HTML summaries, not re-derived; the 'syllabary band 2.0-2.5 after affix stripping' claim is from a secondary voynich.nu/academia summary. User must verify: exact figures before quoting, especially Parisel's 2026 statistics and the Naibbe reproduction list; all output unvalidated until user review.
decisive_tests: Manuscript-length gibberish test: have volunteers (or a Timm-Schinner self-citation generator tuned to observed human behaviour) produce ~38,000 tokens over weeks with illustrations, then run Montemurro & Zanette's information-vs-scale measure (VMS peak ~807 words), Reddy & Knight's ADJPAGESIM (VMS B 38.8%) and Sterneck-style NMF topic/section alignment. Gaskell & Bowern 2022 name this as the untested gap; if gibberish reproduces the section-level structure, the Yale group's main argument for language collapses; if it cannot, the hoax hypothesis loses its last unaddressed feature.

Joint-profile benchmark: require any generator (grille, self-citation, Naibbe-class cipher) to reproduce simultaneously h2 ~2.0-2.2 (EVA), binomial word lengths, Zipf, ~70% hapax types, 0.2-bit final-to-initial glyph MI across boundaries, ~80% end-to-start boundary rate, first/second-word line effects, paragraph-initial gallows in ~85% of paragraphs, and the per-folio ch/sh switch, evaluated separately for Currier A and B. Rozanova & Temerev 2026 and Parisel 2026 publish code and controls for this; a model passing all is decisive for its class, and the two features no model yet passes (edge coupling, hapax rate) are the discriminators to target.

Re-tokenize on 'certain' spaces only: using Rozanova & Temerev's separator classification (uncertain separators 0.494 internality index, image-gap AUC 0.905) and the Zandbergen-Landini transliteration, recompute MATTR/MCW, word-length distribution, Zipf slope and bigram predictability. If the binomial shape and medium-morphology placement survive, word-level language arguments stand; if they collapse into a different distribution, the entire word-level case (Lindemann 2022, B&L §3) rests on an artefact of assumed word boundaries.

Localize the A/B switch: test whether Parisel's per-folio boolean switch aligns with Davis's five hands, with quire/gathering, with illustration section, or is arbitrary per folio. Scribe-aligned = dialect/orthographic habit (compatible with language); quire- or arbitrary-aligned and independent of scribe = cipher-key or generation-parameter behaviour; bimodal within a single scribe's run is strong evidence against a natural dialect reading.

Constrained decipherment attack on the verbose-cipher class: extend Rozanova & Temerev's calibrated substitution attack (null for Voynich) to Naibbe-type many-to-one schemes with a 15th-century Latin/Italian language model; a recovered plaintext segment is decisive for language, while a demonstrated information-theoretic ceiling (ciphertext unigram/bigram capacity insufficient to carry Latin at observed token counts) would be decisive against that cipher class.

Illustration-adjacent word-length test: Gaskell & Bowern observed 17/31 gibberish writers choosing word lengths to fit around drawings; measure whether Voynich tokens abutting illustrations (e.g. f29v) have a length distribution or hapax rate significantly different from mid-paragraph tokens, controlling for line position. A significant fit-to-space effect favours composition without prior text; its absence favours copying/encoding of a pre-existing text.

Cross-scribe consistency of collocations: check whether the few syntagmatic regularities B&L report (qo- words after -y words in B; aiin after 1-2-glyph words; o- before gallows) hold with the same strength across Davis's scribes 2-5 and across quires written at different times. Stable rules across independent hands are hard for intuitive gibberish and unnecessary for self-citation; they are expected for a shared cipher or language.

Independent replication of Gaskell & Bowern with Voynich-like typography: repeat the gibberish protocol using an invented glyph set with positional allographs available, uncontaminated participants, and 1,000+ word samples, then retest the one metric gibberish failed (within-word character-position bias) and the random-forest classification; if uncontaminated writers with allographs reproduce the slot grammar, the last small-scale feature separating Voynichese from gibberish disappears.
